claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy contains a random distribution of multiple metallic elements.
The alloy exhibits normal metallic behavior at room temperature.
The alloy has no confirmed superconducting properties.
The random arrangement of different atomic species creates local lattice distortions and strain fields.
Local lattice distortions and strain fields enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation and drives a superconducting transition.
Thermal annealing reduces atomic disorder in the alloy.
Reducing disorder by annealing diminishes local strain effects.
Diminished local strain weakens or delays the superconducting transition.
The as-cast, more-disordered alloy is expected to undergo a superconducting transition below approximately 5 K at ambient pressure.
The proposed superconducting transition will produce a sharp drop to zero electrical resistance.
The proposed superconducting transition will produce an onset of the Meissner effect.
The annealed, less-disordered counterpart should have a reduced or absent superconducting signature under otherwise identical conditions.
When disorder is too low, local lattice distortions become insufficient to enhance electron–phonon coupling and superconductivity is precluded.
Extremely high disorder can cause carrier localization and suppress superconductivity.
Comparing as-cast and annealed samples through resistance, magnetic-susceptibility, and structural measurements can test the proposed disorder-dependent mechanism.
